title: Tolls In Kind
pitch: A short, sincere essay about how web pages learned to charge for attention sits behind a run of toll gates, and none of them take money. Each gate asks for payment in kind (patience, dignity, spare seconds, a held-still cursor) behind a sign that lies in one specific, learnable way: a decline button worded as a guilt trip, a price list that quietly inverts, fine print that is the real exit. A spotted rule drops the toll and a misread raises the price. Each cleared gate unlocks the next paragraph and a codex card naming the trick, and the run ends with an itemised receipt and a daily seed to compare.
whyNow: Timeless satire of consent banners and paywalls, owed to the humor slot this week. The form-breaking twist is that the interface is the joke and the essay is the prize.

research.summary: Deceptive-design patterns are well catalogued: Brignull's list (confirmshaming, roach motel and others), the five-category academic grouping of nagging, obstruction, sneaking, interface interference and forced action, and the European Data Protection Board's six categories. That gives the gates a real, named rule set to parody. Games about hostile cookie banners already exist (a Berlin university arcade game and a hackathon for the most annoying banners), so this idea differs by making every gate a small hidden-rule puzzle with a different toll currency, gating an actual essay, and by naming the real trick afterwards in a codex.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-12, per Freie Universitaet Berlin event reports, the group built an arcade game, Beat the Cookie Monster, shown at the Long Night of the Sciences (22 July 2024 edition and a later one), where each wrong agreement to a deceptive cookie banner costs one of three lives.

As of 2026-10-12, per the OpenSaaS blog, Wasp ran a contest to build the most irritating cookie consent banner, with the winner picked by community vote; entries included a GDPR quiz, an old-operating-system banner and a find-all-the-cookies banner. Hostile-banner games are a known genre this idea must differ from.
As of 2026-10-12, per search results, Harry Brignull is credited with coining the term dark patterns in 2010 and now uses the term deceptive design; his list includes confirmshaming and roach motel.

As of 2026-10-12, per secondary sources, the Gray et al. (2018) grouping of dark patterns has five categories: nagging, obstruction, sneaking, interface interference and forced action. (The earlier dossier named only the first three.)

As of 2026-10-12, per two explainers, the European Data Protection Board's deceptive design guidelines for social media interfaces (version 2.0 adopted 14 February 2023) name six categories: overloading, skipping, stirring, hindering, fickle and left in the dark.

design.coreLoop: A gate appears with a sign and a price in a play currency. The visitor reads the sign for the lie (which button is real, which number inverts, where the exit hides), pays, negotiates or finds the loophole, and the paragraph behind the gate is revealed. Gates come from 8 rule families, seeded by the URL hash, so each run reshuffles the tricks and prices. The loop rewards the second minute (recognising a family) and the tenth (reading faster for a lower receipt and filling the codex).
sophisticationHooks: Seeded gate generator: 8 rule families by 2 skins each (a third if time remains), with price curves that rise on a misread and fall on a correct read, deterministic from the hash
Three play currencies (patience, dignity, spare seconds) with different spend mechanics; explicitly no real money or payment fields
Codex that names the real trick after each gate, tying the joke to the documented taxonomy with 'as of' dating
Itemised receipt and daily-seed compare, with an always-visible 'skip with shame' escape hatch that logs a costume-drama penalty
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: 8 gate families with 2 skins each (16 short interactions, each solvable in under 15 seconds; a third skin only if time remains), seeded generator, wallet and receipt, 8-paragraph essay, codex with localStorage (try/catch, optional), keyboard and touch alternatives for every gate, about/making-of panel listing the sources. Cut: sound beyond a few procedural blips, multiplayer, any real payment look-alike, any real brand or banner imitation, third skins.
risks: Prior art: banner-rejection games exist (FU Berlin, Wasp hackathon); differentiate through hidden-rule puzzles, the essay prize and the codex.
Frustration by design can tip into just being annoying: cap each gate's time, add the skip-with-shame hatch, keep the tone warm.
Accessibility: hold-still and timing gates need non-motor alternatives and reduced-motion variants.
Humor-satire/game neighbours in today's pool (the carried-over Breaking Changes idea) share the satire tone; this one is a puzzle in the weird-experimental category with different form.
No real company banners or logos: all brands invented, all marks drawn.

Unverified sources: the University of Washington slides, the arXiv study 2412.09147, the UX Planet article and the Bejamas count of 12 could not be found again; the codex and about panel cite only sources 6 to 12, and any other taxonomy line is shown as 'as of 2026-10-12, per <source>' or omitted.
Scope: 16 gates is the ceiling for one morning; builders ship families in priority order so a half-finished family is cut rather than shipped rough.

verification.notes: Prior art and the dark-pattern taxonomies were re-found by independent searches, but no page was opened and three original sources (UW slides, arXiv 2412.09147, UX Planet) could not be found again. Shrunk to 16 gates; the concept has real depth and no guardrail issue (invented brands, no money, no personal data).
